utterances.text: That is not correct. I did consider this, I think, as a contemporary historian would do, to try to look at all the different sources and assess the situation. But it is, of course, correct that I am not specialised in military issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have used the words "contemporary historian." Could you list all the courses in the subject of history --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need to go through that. The witness was using an expression, not meaning literally a contemporary historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: For your convenience, I may mention that it's listed on my curriculum vitae that I had one year of study related to old history, but there are some courses in history as well, Roman culture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Moving on to Prosecution Exhibit 18, that is a statement of several military officers of the army of Republika Srpska; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's particularly two people who are quoted and referred to, Colonel Radmilo Zeljaja and Pero Colic. Excuse me for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have emphasised certain aspects of this article. I'm directing your attention to the full paragraph 2. You don't have to read it out loud, just read it for yourself and then we will have some questions.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is the meaning of Prince Lazar to the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I think he is rightly venerated as one of their most noble, outstanding persons in history. He died at the battlefield of Kosovo Polje in 1389 when the Turks were invading.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the battle of Kosovo Polje with Prince Lazar dying in battle. Do you know what happened to, and I would use the term, "Ottoman Empire," because Turkey is a nation today that is not a successor to the Ottoman empire, except in the historical sense. What happened to the commanding officer of the opposing army of the Ottoman Empire at Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Excuse me. What had happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened to the Turkish sultan who opposed Prince Lazar at Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I believe I don't know that particular historical person, but as they came to power in the region, after that, I believe those who opposed Prince Lazar somehow invaded the area. Maybe I misunderstood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I will state it. The Ottoman Empire was coming on to the Balkans, and the decisive battle whether they would invade the Balkans or not at that time was on Kosovo Polje. I asked the name of the Turkish sultan and what happened to him because you brought it up. If I may jog your memory, his name was Sultan Murat. Do you know what happened to him at Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, we're now getting rather far away from the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I should, perhaps, apologise, but I have not taken the time to go into detail about the complex and, I'm sure, also a very interesting and important history of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Indeed, there is a particular meaning in Serb history that is tied up to the Kosovo battle, and you have testified to the meaning of that day in Tadic's case. You're quite aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I know that I have mentioned also the battle of Kosovo Polje in the Tadic case. I am not --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: St. Vitus's Day, as you said and Ragodsaj Vivodan, if that would help you?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, St. Vitus is a saint and King Lazar died on the day of this saint. So in celebrating that day, one also celebrates the loss of the life of King Lazar at Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This article has been printed on the day which basically the army of Republika Srpska took as their day of glory, and that day was what? Because you testified from this article, and the article --

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: The article is dated 1st of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I direct your attention in the second line of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, I have read that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the statements made on the glory day of the Serb army, which was the same day as Vidovdan is traditionally a day of glory or day of martyrdom of Serb people?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: This is how I read and understand the article and it would fit with the history, as far as I know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Just to take these statements in the proper context, when two military commanders are talking to the troops, at least in the countries that do have a long, long span of history, they do refer to some of the glory days of their national past. That would be entirely proper?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm directing your attention to the last two sentences on the paragraph on page 1 beginning with "Fate has decided"; can you read that out loud?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Excuse me, the last two --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The last two paragraphs on the first page of Exhibit 18. That's "The Glory of all Serb Glories."

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Does it start with "But our honourable"?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It starts, "Fate has decided St. Vitus Day to be the day," the last paragraph on the first page, the bottom two sentences.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Excuse me, yes, I've found it now. "Fate has decided that St. Vitus Day is to be the day of the Serbian truth and because of that the Serbs will win this third World War, too, although it is being waged only against the Serbs. We will win because we have firmly decided not to live any longer in brotherhood with those who slaughter our children and with false brothers who have spat several times at Serbian goodness and decency." Did you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, no. So in making such a statement, a military officer could reasonably make the statement believing that it is true what he is saying? You, in other words --

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I am not suggesting that he is not believing what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In other words, you're suggesting that what he is saying, that we have no reason to doubt that he is, that he is speaking what he believes to be the truth?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: He is speaking the way he sees things and finds it suitable to present it to his troops, yes. I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am asking you to read Paragraph No. 2, starting, "If that honourable Serb nobleman had done that."

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: "It's not only that that honourable Serb nobleman had done that, when you're saying to King Lazar, the Serbian men and people would have disappeared exactly 605 years ago, the world would have lacked the most tolerant and greatest people on the entire planet. In that case, freedom would look different and Europe would look different today."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: From a historical perspective, what is he relating to?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I think he is relating again to the decisive, as you explained it, battle at Kosovo Polje. And he is telling them that this was an achievement and that there are good causes for celebrating this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In making the statement, are you aware that the Ottoman Empire reigned Serbian people for 500 years?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that statement is, that historical fact is figured in his statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: This is correct. I believe it was together with Russian brothers and the peace settlement of 1888 that finally they were withdrawn from the area completely, Serbian area, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am going to get a map here now. If I may have this map displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which exhibit number is that, please, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's No. 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: It's 17, I believe. Could we have it displayed on the overhead projector, so that the judges could see it. I mean, if it would be easier. If the Judges do have a map, we can look on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were collected yesterday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Cassese points out quite rightly, this is the one that was withdrawn, in fact, for the Prosecution to do some redaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have copies of it. What is the point that you're seeking --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The point was that the term, Krajina, because I was under the misapprehension that it was admitted only to the fact that it was a map and all other statements were stricken. But it seems, you know, that it was withdrawn, I didn't get a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point about it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The point is if I could use only this to aid and assist the witness with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This is your own drawing, Dr. Greve, right, these markings, in yellow, right?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: The yellow is my marking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And you have used statement, Krajina, Bosanska Krajina and Croatian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And do you know the meaning within a historical context of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, you must understand that this Trial Chamber now has some experience of these matters. And, of course, we're not going to stop you exploring things which are necessary, but these are matters which I think that we are familiar with. So there is no need to go over Krajina, unless there is some particular point that you want to make about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed within the context of the statement of Colonel Colic is where he is using that in that case freedom would look different and Europe would look differently today. It's within that context that I am going to use -- to explain what he has meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. If you would move on from the history as soon as you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact -- I will go and I will try to assist with this very quickly to the witness if I may, Your Honour. If you're aware that Krajina is a term translated as a military district. And that the -- after the Ottoman invasion of the Balkan peninsula, that over the centuries there were the constant clashes between Christian monarchies to the north and Ottoman muslims to the south. And the Serbian population being a Christian that were always sided and protected their co-faith neighbours to the north. And, in turn, the Hungarians, Austrians and Italians to the west have supplied and helped Serbia in their long resistance to the Turkish occupation. Therefore, that was all of those areas starting from Belgrade along river Sava into the northwestern Bosnia, that was all called Krajina, meaning military district. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I listened to your explanation and I have no reason to question it, but I have to admit, I did not know the Krajina as name used when the Ottoman Empire advanced after 1389, but I do know and I do appreciate and I think Europe is grateful for what the Serb people has done as being sort of guardian of the borders with the Ottoman Empire and has stopped the advance of the Ottoman Empire.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And within that, since we have understanding on that point, I just wanted to say, is it reasonable to conclude that Colonel Colic was referring to that fact in that statement? A fact of which a Serb people are proud and you indicated that, perhaps, Europe is grateful?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have no reason not to share Europe's feelings about what the Serbs have done for the European community in a historical perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question was, is that what the general or the colonel was referring to? And it appears that it was. So I think, Mr. Vucicevic, you -- just a moment. These are all matters which we will have to consider in due course. It will be for us to interpret the documents. All the witness can do is produce them. If you want to make any particular points, of course, you're free to do so, but perhaps we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: There is in this article, for the first time, we come across the term "corridor". And that's on page 2, in the middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I am afraid that it was taken away from me, so maybe I could have it again. Forgive me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to repeat the reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The second page of the Prosecutor's Exhibit No. 18, the last paragraph, which starts with, "In the operation to open the so-called corridor." And you can just read it for yourself and I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with the fact that that corridor was closed, militarily, at the end of April or beginning of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I am not familiar with it as being closed. That is to say, I am familiar with it being a battlefield. So when war was waged, there may have been opening and closing. I did not specifically consider the entirety of the corridor at every different time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So, basically, you just referred in your testimony to corridor, but you're not familiar with the military significance or any other significance of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I am familiar with the significance of it, but I am not familiar with day by day, the size of the corridor, it being fully open or open in part, being fought over. I know it was a battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So, since you testified yesterday, the corridor was important to the Serbs. If I ask a hypothetical question, tell you, that corridor was closed militarily by Muslims and Croats and that Bosnian, that Bosnian Serbs were encircled, would that help you explain the statements that you have just read, there were military operations to break down the blockade? Could that make sense?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That could make sense, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You, in the next exhibit, I mean the Prosecutor's Exhibit 19, you have made remarks to the JNA and the connection between SDS and JNA. At the time that war in Croatia was being waged, the Bosnia and Herzegovina were a state, a federal unit of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the authorities of any nation, sovereign nation, could issue a mobilisation orders, could they?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And in all civilised countries, there are penalties for not responding to the mobilisation order, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That's normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And in the times of war, the civilian authorities and political authorities have to cooperate within the bounds of the laws of that country as a general proposition?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That is the normal situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes. And, at that time, the citizens of Prijedor, who responded to the mobilisation orders, they lawfully carried out their duties, correct?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the war in Croatia ended in December, roughly, December/November, end of November, beginning of December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I believe there was a formal cease fire agreement beginning of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the old JNA troops after that time were being pulled out?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: They were being withdrawn from Croatia. To what extent there were any left, I have not the full knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So SDS was a party, one of the political parties in Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And as the general proposition, the Serbs mostly responded to this mobilisation, correct?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That is all the information I have seen, yes. At least my information is limited to Prijedor and the information I have on that is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the most of the population that didn't respond to this mobilisations, these mobilisation order were Croats and Muslims, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: These were people who declared themselves as Croats and Muslims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And refused to carry out the orders of their, at that time, independent countries, the country of which they were citizens and subject to the laws?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is it fair to conclude that this caused a great discord among those two or three entities, at least, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: It may well have been a reason for that. I also think that the entire war in Croatia was reason for people disagreeing or looking differently at that war.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In this article you also used a term being called a "Turk" is a derogatory for a Bosnian Muslim. Are you sure, absolutely sure about that?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: My understanding from the Muslims is that they prefer to be called Bosniaks, Muslims, Prijedorians, whatever, but not to be referred to with the name of an alien people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: But is that was their preference as of the later date, perhaps with the modern history that you're testifying on, or we could look at just a little bigger expansion. Let's say from 1945 to '95, when the relationship among the citizens of Prijedor were normal. Perhaps that could be, hypothetical again, most of the Muslim population of Bosnia is Slav population that converted to Islam throughout Ottoman times, you would agree on that, would you?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Okay. So for somebody who was an original faith, it perhaps, could be a compliment to be called, you are a Turk? If you know, and if you don't, you can say so.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: As to my understanding as Defence counsel rightly pointed out, in the early days, it was the incoming Ottoman Empire and not a Turkish state. And it is my understanding that those who, and I have spoken to some people on this issue because it was not sort of -- I read it in the testimonies that they saw it as derogative. And I have spoken with people on a general basis on the issue later and they say that they did not find it good. And it had not been common to speak about Muslims as Turks and it was not appreciated. That's my understanding. I have just not spoken to people just after World War II, which was, of course, prior to my time. And also, if I may, Turkish history during World War II, possibly made it less pleasant for anyone to be referred to as Turkish considering that the Partisans took power and ruled Yugoslavia after 1945.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now I am a little bit at sea with that statement. If you would, I cannot see a connection between Partisans and--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going quite away from the main point of this case. Can we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, you might have been referring in your last statement, perhaps World War I, not World War II and activities of Turkey and independent nations and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It really doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the same article, you are, the same article contains in the, "For the good of the people." And if you could read that paragraph and I will have three or four questions because I think it's rather important.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Excuse me, would you advise me where I find it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On the page 2, Exhibit 19. Midsection titled, "For the good of the people." Second paragraph in that subheading, starting with, "From the very start."

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have read the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with the name Jovan Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court who was he?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I know that he was an SDS leader in Krajina. Krajina in this context being the Croat part of Krajina. And he was a Serb, who was, at the time, a Croat national, living in Croatia that was. And he was one of the people who early spoke up for the Serb cause in that region as a politician.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was he a nationalist, a Serb nationalist?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I am hesitant to use the word --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That will be fine. Quite so, you know, I appreciate your hesitancy on this question. We can define a nationalism as the good nationalism and bad nationalism. And I would say the good nationalism is somebody who appreciates his own culture, history, population, but at the same time doesn't want to hurt others living in their midst or the people who are willing to give him them the same civil rights, if reciprocity exists. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt that he was all in favour of the good of his own people. If he was unprepared to hurt anyone else and give them full rights, I have no basis for ascertaining.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: But you don't know anything else besides what you just stated of the late Dr. Jovan Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: No, I have seen references to him in several articles. I believe I have read some of his early writings in articles. But as it did not concern aspects of what I then was addressing, I have not paid so strong attention to it that I would be able to repeat it or inform the Court about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Within this section here, he is considered like the ideological father of SDS in Prijedor; isn't he?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I did not read the paragraph to make him the ideological father. I read him, I read the paragraph to praise him for having been visionary and having been positive for the cause of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I were to -- let's assume the fact that the late Dr. Jovan Raskovic was present when SDS was established in Prijedor. And if I were to tell you that fact that his wife is still living is a Croatian, would he have less base to assume that he was a vitriolic nationalist?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object on a technical point as to the statement that's being made. If it's a hypothetical that these are facts, then perhaps that's a further question. What he is stating as a fact is he is, in essence, testifying and I would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, he can put matters -- and, counsel, I should say, I do deprecate the use of he. Mr. Vucicevic, if you're referring to him. Mr. Vucicevic, you can put the matter, but if you're putting it as a fact, you should do so or if it's a hypothesis. Again, I don't know that we're going to much assisted by this. This is going to be comments by the witness on matters which she really knows nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, it's in the same paragraph, Dr. Greve, there are two terms mentioned. And one that prominently comes to mind of anybody who is familiar with the history of Balkan is Jasenovac, what is Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Jasenovac is a concentration camp. One of the worst. Definitely the worst in World War II, located not so far from Prijedor on the border inside Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am going to interrupt you. We are familiar with these matters. In a case we have recently done, there was extensive evidence about Jasenovac, so there is no need to go over that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. As the legal principles and due processes we are applying here. And then I am asking, not some latitude, but the concern that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can make any point that you want, but would you bear in mind that we have heard evidence in other matters about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this witness was not present there and when that evidence was introduced and this witness' testimony contains those statements and she has testified to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not waste any more time about it. The only point I want you to have in mind is that the Trial Chamber is not ignorant of the history, is familiar with it, and so, therefore, what I am concerned about is that we don't spend too much time going over matters which are not going to assist us in the long run in trying the case because we know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Having heard this ruling, Dr. Greve, I have to point out in the Tadic's testimony, you have testified about the influence of the Serb press to the media, on to the state of mind of the Serb population in Prijedor area, have you?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And and what was the influence of the Serb press on the state of mind of the citizens of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: The understanding which is given from the witness statements from all of the sources is that opposed to previous years, one starts speaking about the Muslims as being people prepared as fanatics to start a religious war. And one refers to the Croats as being hands to the very, very bad Ustasha behavior.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you, please, explain who were Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Ustashas, to my knowledge, was first a minority party. Perhaps it was with past religion in Croatia. It was -- its leaders were more or less living in fascist Italy and raised by the fascists in Italy. And when the Germans started World War II, they came into power in then independent Croatia, which also covered Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they had an extreme, terrible, utterly ugly policy of treating all Serbs extremely bad. That is, I believe they had as part of their programme, that they wanted to convert one-third of the Serbs to the Roman Catholic faith, whilst to excise one-third of the Serbs. And, even worse, to exterminate the final third of the Serbs. That is all Serbs living within that area. As it came out in Prijedor, if I may draw your attention to that, is an area that was early controlled by the Partisan and suffered tremendously in 1942. At that time, it is my information, that the Germans, the Austrians, at the time, of course, one time, met the Secretary-General of the United Nations who was number two in the command in Banja Luka. So this is an area that's been sort of investigated by a number of different, not so open sources, but it has been investigated. And this joint forces, Austrian, German, Ustasha and a fraction of the Chetnik movement, not all Chetniks, but also a fraction of the Chetniks, committed extreme atrocities in 1942, July of 1942, in the Prijedor area, which is why one of the main monuments, war monuments and memorials in former Yugoslavia, from World War II, was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Jasenovac was just in the same area, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: It's a bit further to the east and the North. It's on the other side of the Croatian border. Yes, well, I could point it out on a map, but it's further north and east. But it's in the same larger area, not within the opstina, not within Bosnia-Herzegovina, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: About 30 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I would have guessed more, but...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Prijedor, if you think of it, the size of Prijedor, it's perhaps something like 25 by 30 kilometres, so somehow a rectangular shape. But this is approximate of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned Ustasha and also mentioned the context of this paragraph is that they had a policy of exterminating at least one-third of the Serbian people. And that's what I understand in the history and tell me if you agree with me, that they were exterminating regardless, men, women and children?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That's my understanding, absolutely. And I would not be surprised if they have actually also exterminated more than they had in their programme. Their policy was utterly inhumane.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: One minor point that you mentioned that the former Secretary General of the United Nations was a second in command in that area and that event was investigated, but not as openly as perhaps it should have been to give the picture to the world of what had happened, if you agree?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I don't know why the information about such investigations were not disclosed, but such investigations were carried out. And, in my opinion, it would have been fair to publish information also about what had happened during World War II. When I said he was number two within the intelligence unit, number two in command in Banja Luka. I have heard that that's number three in the overall command. I am not able to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And you are aware there was some survivors from those Ustasha camps around surrounding Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I am aware of that and also, very unfortunately, but people from Prijedor after the slaughter, after the horrors of July of 1942, was taken in part to Jasenovac, but some of them were actually also taken under the label "viking" to my country, which is Norway as slave labour, taken to the Nazi minority government in Norway and treated extremely badly. I did gather from sources in Belgrade the exact lists of all the names of people who came to Norway from the Prijedor area after what had happened in 1942. The majority of those were Serbs, but there were also Croats and Muslims among them. Very unfortunately, but a number died in my country.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the ruling from those great sufferings of the former, of the internees in the Nazi camps, in Norway, subsequently, there was, you know, a friendship, associations formed between people of Norway and people in Yugoslavia and quite a few visits have taken place, if you followed anything there?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar; yes, I followed; yes, there is a strong friendship between the people of the former Yugoslavia and Norway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, we'll adjourn now. How much longer do you anticipate being with this witness, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are going to review the facts of the exhibits with this witness and maybe, perhaps, Mr. Vann will ask a few questions because in preparing for this witness, we have had the first statement. And we are thinking, you know, that he was going to do a cross-examination. But, however, when the exhibits were introduced and Mr. Vann had come in just about ten, fifteen days ago, then I have to go over these statements because, you know, I have been on the case from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter. But as a matter of practice, only one cross-examination is going to be allowed. I'll consider an application if you want to make one. But the normal practice is one cross-examination per defendant. I hope that matters can be speeded. Obviously this witness is here, having to stay here. And also, we have to think of the clock generally for the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate your kind words. Your Honour, this is the first witness testifying on issues and the ultimate issues of fact in historical terms, quite candid witness, and I believe her function to aid the Court to see that most objects the picture. That is our intent. And if it takes a little longer, Your Honour, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Five past two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: While we have a short intermission, if I may answer the question on citations, I asked the witness about methodology earlier. That's at page 609 from the Tadic transcript and it's line 29. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We had left off with the statements about Serbian media and the reporting of the current events. In introducing Mr. Mazowiecki's report, you have testified that Serb media in Prijedor, as far as you were concerned, being your area of expertise, have been inflammatory, derogatory, and reports that were inciting people to genocide. Is that a fair conclusion of your testimony of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That was inciting people to have a less good view on other people in the opstina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So it was not your testimony that the press was inciting them to commit violations of international humanitarian law, but were contributing to a lack of goodwill towards the different ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: It was not directly suggesting that they should commit genocide, it was not putting words like that, but it was spoken of in a very hostile manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We can take the general proposition that we all believe in free press; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Even if some events might be unpleasant and might present as offensive to the opposing ethnic group, if they are reported, they are still subject to this interpretation of free press, as a general proposition?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: In general, yes, if the press is free, one may print different issues in it. This is one element in an overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Considering Yugoslavia from 1945 through 1990, to the best of your knowledge, did Yugoslavia have a free press?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I'm not fully familiar with the freedom of the press. I would think that it was not fully free, but I'm not able to evaluate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: But for the short period of democracy in Prijedor, we can say the press was free?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I think the press changed its approach because it was made, to the best of my understanding, a matter of urgency for the new authorities, that is, the Serb authorities, after taking power the night of the 30th of April, 1992, to have control over the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: However, you have testified only as to the Mazowiecki report, you have testified only as to bias in Serb media. Have you noticed anything in that report that addressed the possible bias in the media of the other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: It is referring to numerous concerns, yes. I was particularly evaluating the information that could relate to the problems I was addressing in the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So if you look at the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that report, it would seem that press from all sides was biased?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: It's indicated by Mazowiecki that there were problems, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you consider it a bias if the Serb press is referring to the events of Jasenovac that you earlier testified? Would that be a bias or would that be a reporting of the historical events?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: If it's mainly reporting the historical events, there is no bias. It may be a bias if, without documentation, it is stated that a new Jasenovac is being considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you found any statements that said that a new Jasenovac is being considered? You can answer that at some time later. We don't have to look now, but it would be interesting to find out. If I may proceed, we can put it off until later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: It is in paragraph -- as I read, if I may, on page 2 in what was given to me prior to the -- it's Exhibit 19, the Kozarski Vjesnik article "Faithful to the Homeland and its Ideals," page 2, second paragraph underneath the headline "For the Good of the People," and I quote from the second sentence: "We used all our resources to support the struggle of the Serb people against new and old ustashas, against the new genocide which was being prepared in places that are too well known to us, Jasenovac, Jadovna," et cetera, reference to the past is not biased, but it may be different when one suggests that there were plans to build or to continue in the way things were done during World War II.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So if the author of this paragraph or the gentleman that was quoted to have said such a paragraph, Mr. Ranko Gnjatovic, had veritable apprehension at the time that the camps like Jasenovac could occur, he didn't have a right to speak about it or didn't have a right to report about it; is that what you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- as incitement through the press?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: If he had information to that extent, of course he would be not only free to speak about it, but he should speak about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: But you haven't talked, as you said before, to any of the Serbs, so we really cannot conclude whether or not at this point there was such information. That is your opinion, that he had no information, without any data to substantiate that?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have not seen in all the sources I've reviewed any concrete information as to that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Let's go to Mazowiecki's report. When it's dealing with the reporting of the Bosnian Muslim press, especially Radio Hajat, do you remember that section of Mazowiecki's report?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not because I did not attempt to, sort of, judge all of his statements on every issue. I believe that Mazowiecki has solid reason for saying many of the things that he was saying. I was testifying yesterday to what he had said about the media. It's dated after I finished my report, but it does support the conclusions to which I reached concerning media in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm referring you to page 9 or date stamped 790 on the bottom of Mazowiecki's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the exhibit. It's Exhibit 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 32, I'm directing your attention to the last sentence starting "On 1 April 1993." Could you read that statement, please?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: On 1 April 1993, the Tuzla journal Zmaj od Bosne published an article which stated, "Instinctively, every Muslim would wish to save his Serb neighbour instead of the reverse; however, every Muslim must name a Serb and take an oath to kill him."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Looking at the plain language of that statement, does it sound to you as an incitement to break international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And it was published on?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: 1st April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Zmaj od Bosne is the print media published in Tuzla which was, at that time, under Bosnian government control, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I don't know, but if you stated this like this, I accept that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 30, the same page, last sentence in that paragraph 30, "An example was Radio Hajat ..." Could you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Would you like me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: An example was Radio Hajat's call on 5th February, 1994 following the massacre at Markale marketplace for Muslims to retaliate against Sarajevo's Serbs and Croats."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you read this paragraph before you testified yesterday on it?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The whole report?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have read the whole report at a previous time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right. Are you familiar with Markale marketplace massacre?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I am familiar with the overall of that, yes. It was also included in the report of the Commission of Experts, although I was not the one who was particularly looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us about that massacre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, again --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The sentence that you just read, looking at the plain meaning of the language, to the best of your expertise, does it incite and invite the population of Sarajevo to commit violations of the international humanitarian laws against Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: It's an invitation to retaliation, and I would assume that means also to break the law, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may address on this specific point. We have an expert here on international humanitarian law, and I would like to ask her to clarify the term "retaliate" because of her stature. I really wouldn't want this to go on the record uncorrected for the learned benefit of all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you can ask the question, but keep it brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Under international humanitarian law, is retaliation a measure even arguably permitted by a civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: To my knowledge, retaliation, as such, is not a part of international law. One may not answer to a crime, I'm speaking in general terms without reference to Sarajevo or anywhere else, one may not answer a crime with a new crime. There may be occasions of provocation, but retaliation is not a concept that's included in international law and duly described. But since they are asked to retaliate in terms of a massacre, I'm afraid this could include new crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So is it or isn't it incitement to commit violations of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: As it's not stated explicitly that no crimes should be made, it may be read like you're stating, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's sufficient on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In your previous testimony, you have said that the violation of international humanitarian law in the Prijedor area throughout World War II has been committed by Ustasha and supported by the government at that time, the independent government of Croatia. Were there any incidents that you know of where similar acts were committed by Serb nationals on Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have read wartime history. I am aware that certain Chetnik groups, not all Chetniks, by far not, would target explicitly Muslim people in some areas. I am not able to point to, in detail, specific incidents from World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Judge Greve, you are not here really to deal with World War II, and I'm not going to permit any more questions on it. Mr. Vucicevic, could you move on, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Judge Greve, you have testified in your statement about peacefulness and brotherhood between ethnicities in Prijedor. Could you explain the meaning of "brotherhood" and where it came into the modern historical terminology?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: To my understanding, there were very friendly relations between the different groups in Prijedor. That is to say, it was not an area which was troubled by ethnic feuds or religious feuds. They were living together as people in any ordinary community or society which would not have much differences between them. It's my understanding that they themselves saw at least this century as having been a century of botherhood, which had been particularly strengthened during World War II, as this was an area where, as an example, the Muslim head of the community very early spoke up and against the Ustasha attacks on Serbs in World War II, and where the Partisans comprised of the local population which were Serbs, the majority were Serbs, Croats and Muslims. For what reason they fought together during World War II, and some of the people that have testified had said that even upon entering Logor Omarska, Logor Keraterm, the camps, they did not really think those who were arrested, having not experienced attacks on entire villages, that this would be something very difficult for them. Even after the Serbs took power, the ousted Muslim mayor of the community spoke on the radio, Radio Prijedor, in early May saying "Remember the brotherhood, sisterhood," perhaps he didn't say that, but "... brotherhood, remember the good relations. There are people coming from outside. They have taken power. We have nothing to fear. This is essentially a peaceful community." By this, I'm not suggesting that it didn't have the same kinds of problems that just any community would have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The concept brotherhood was imposed by the communists taking over power in 1945, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I know that the word "brotherhood" is used in my own country, which has never been --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: But I am referring directly to the concept of Bosnia, brotherhood is very broad term?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That is why I -- without knowing it for sure, cannot say that this was brought in by the communists, it's a very common concept. Perhaps, at least, I would assume it existed in the wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So, at least, you're not sure on this question?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: No, I have not asked specifically when the concept brotherhood was started to be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: But yet in presenting statistics, did it raise some concerns of yours to realise that most of the villages were entirely Muslim, entirely Serb and entirely Croats?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how could you reconcile brotherhood and in unity with such segregation?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: If I may draw your attention again back to the statistics from the census. I believe it can be read out of the figures, not so easily from the simplified map, but from the figures that in almost every village, you would find a mixed population --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Let's go back to the tables, Dr. Greve, and then maybe we can explain this better to the Court. And I am directing your attention to -- okay, that's page 202 or that is Exhibit 21B. And then we go -- let's look at village called Bistrica. That is the third row from the bottom of the page. Date stamped 201. And it does have 1490 Serbs and 1 Muslim. And then if we go to a next village, Biscani, we have a little better ratio, 1150 Muslims and 2 Serbs. And let's look at some other, bigger villages. That would be at page 203 because it seems that this is a big spread which has been cut?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That's correct. It's two opposite pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if we take a look at the village Carakovo, where there is 2128 Muslims and 38 Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Those figures, I think, are in 1981, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: 1981. But they have been introduced and I believe, substantially, they have not changed, Your Honour. But we can go into the '91 census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am not inviting you to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: But basically I am drawing your attention here and I want to find out the names of these villages.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: The names are listed on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Here we go. And there is, for example, a village, Surkovac, which contains 647 Croats; no Muslims and 18 Serbs. This is not a statistically representative sample, however, it's just indication, there was no integration whatsoever of the population, in spite of that catch phrase "brotherhood," isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: As I read the entire statistics, I think it's much more mixed than the history samples suggested. But, yes, it's correct, there will be a lot of variations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And as I have a duty of fairness to the Court, I am going to point out to the town of Prijedor, which basically the population was about 50/50. Okay. That's on date stamp 205 and then it's '81. We're still looking at '81. But that is 10,000 Muslims at that time and 10,000 Serbs. '91 there was about 24,000 Serbs. However there is this category of Yugoslavs. Could you tell the Court a little bit more about that category?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That was a category which does not state which ethnic group or religion the person has. People may want to declare themselves as Yugoslavs belonging to any other group. Where they have the freedom of choice in that respect, many would choose the designation Yugoslav as a commitment to the Yugoslav state. Others have chosen that for the reason that they may have two grandparents in one group and one in each of the others, not feeling they belonged, perhaps, to any specific group. And some may have, for any other reason, found it good not to be identified with a group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Isn't it fair, also reasonable to conclude there might be one reason and one conclusion. But it would be another reasonable conclusion that a census at that time provided for the people to declare how they feel and whom they belong. And what we see that most of those villages and hamlets are exclusively, overwhelmingly, either Serb, Muslim or Croat without any mix in municipality besides town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: As for the mix, I think the figures speak for themselves. I mean, it could be controlled village by village the exact numbers according to the figure. It is correct that people were free to come forward and declare themselves as belonging to a group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would it be also reasonable to conclude that mixing in the rural areas did not occur because of the memories on the atrocities of the World War II?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That is not to my opinion correct. It may not in full, it may be in part. That is, there are a number of people who have left Prijedor who have mixed family relationships, mixed parentage and, perhaps also, as we came across, decided to declare themselves when they married someone from a different group they could, as well, declare themselves as belonging with that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So they have basically converted and declared themselves. And one of those famous, one of the most famous Yugoslavs who converted, if you know, was a Yugoslav Nobel prize winner for the literature, Ivanovic. And he was born Croat, but declared himself Serb and one of the Serbs greatest literary giants. Are you familiar with that? So we agree that the people do convert for their own reason and, indeed, join the other ethnic group. But as we are looking in these papers here, their declarations are such that this is overwhelming segregation in all the areas or municipality of Prijedor, besides Prijedor itself?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I do not agree that it's overwhelming segregation in all the areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am going to modify that term. Segregation that is of some concern. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Considering that they had official policy of brotherhood?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I think that brotherhood could be understood in more than one sense. And I think a feeling of brotherhood may mean that people in an area with several villages, several different administrative units, do not feel alienated and hostile towards one another, but still they may keep their small hamlets, or whatever, which is -- and some of those which you have pointed out, are predominantly with people declaring themselves as belonging to one particular group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That reminds me of the old adage, that in the former communist system some people are more free than the others. And it seems here that distribution or ethnic distribution in Prijedor municipality is such that they trusted their own a little bit more than the others, so they had their houses in the same location, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I will not be able, as I have not asked people that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you on that one. When you look to this answer to this one might become indeed obvious when you look at the map of Prijedor. This map of Prijedor. Sorry, I lost the marking on this one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So when you look at the colour distribution here, it's obvious to see that the Muslims were located in a south-western section of the Municipality of Prijedor and Serbs were located in southeastern municipality of Prijedor. And there is a great concentration of Muslim population in Kozarusa, Kozarac, Brdani, Babici area. Those are along the road. There is no road there, but you are familiar with the maps along the road from Prijedor to Banja Luka. And there is a concentration of the Serbs again straight north from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, that is the simplification and the predominant ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And yet on the next exhibit, which is your drawing, it's Exhibit 24, you have declared that Prijedor and municipalities in Prijedor and Sanski Most and Kotor Varos are the Muslim municipalities. What did you mean -- what is your intended purpose of this different colouration?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: The different colouration refers to the fact that the opstinas, the municipalities that have been given a red colour had such a large Serb influence, not a total Serb population, but such a large Serb influence, that it was decided within the opstina to join the autonomous region of Krajina as referred to yesterday, as opposed to the three others opstinas, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kotor Varos, while, yes, there were large populations that were Serbs. There were small populations, essentially Croat. And there were relatively large populations that were Muslim. And in these three opstinas, municipalities, the Serb influence was not that strong that a decision was made by the local authorities to join the autonomous region of Krajina. That was the only reason for giving them different colours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am going to take you back to time of election in 1990, December of 1990. And the result of that election was, as you have testified in Tadic's case and your report that was introduced in this case, that the SDA had obtained 30 electoral seats; that the SDS had 28; Croat party had 2 seats and the others, meaning the parties who were liberal parties or remnants and followers of the old communist left, obtained another 30 seats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that members of SDA and SDS formed a coalition municipal government in Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: The municipal assembly, I think reflected the overall vote, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: But there was an agreement between SDA and SDS to run the coalition campaign against the ruling communist party up to that time. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I am not familiar with pre-1990 election campaigning. But I am familiar with the fact that, yes, the SDA and the SDS did cooperate, did win 30 and 28 seats respectfully and did divide the remaining seats among them accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You're not familiar with any pre-election agreements. Let's say no agreements existed as a hypothetical and the election takes place and this is an electoral composition, the government has to be formed. So each party had free choice. SDA could join the communist parties or reformist liberal SD socialist party and another party, or they could join the SDS in forming government. Likewise, SDS couldn't join parties of the left that were defeated in that election or let's say there was almost three way split. Why would you think that SDA and SDS would make such a coalition?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I would assume that also that naturally under the circumstances, if it was a reaction to the previous regimes, I am unable to say. But I would assume that under the new political situation, they saw that as useful and making sense, the way they have committed themselves with the veto voters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And those commitments in taking down to totalitarian government, which did not recognise a right to free religious expression, would be reasonable to assume that members of SDA wanted to have democratically elected officers and to practice their religion. At the same time, members or the people having sympathies in voting for the representatives of the SDS would like to have democratically elected government and to practice their religion. And those would be including another underlining theme that democratically elected government would provide the bulwark for the economy so that the society would thrive. Based on those principles, is it reasonable to assume that they have formed coalition government?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Based on what we know in general about what happened in eastern Europe, when free elections started, there were to be close cooperation between political parties that were of the new political creed, so to speak and those parties who preferred the previous system. So I would assume in Prijedor, making a general statement, that is, and it's an assumption, I would think they would work together with those who believed in the new, free situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So it's reasonable to assume that even those who are members of the party at that time did not harbour ill-feelings toward each other because they were cooperating? I am not asking the specifics, just, would it be reasonable to assume.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: It is, of course, difficult to assess the feelings of people. But since the general understanding in Prijedor is that of brotherhood and cooperation, I assume that was for the politicians as well. It may have changed over time, but I think so. But I think the main changes may have come when parallel structures started to come into being.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you think that war in Croatia preceded those improvisations along the ethnic lines starting with the outbreak of war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I know that there were political discussions about, and I believe they are materialised in guidelines which I have seen later, only after having completed my study. There were discussions within the SDS, the Serb Democratic Party, already in August, 1991. That is just after the -- just before or just after the war in Croatia really started. And at that time, alternative structures were in question. I am in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You think -- do you have any information that an ethnic cleansing of Serb population took place in the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I have information to the extent that when war started in Eastern Slavonia, group was against group, and yes, indeed, some of the victims were clearly Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you think that such an information could have had a real impact on the Serbs in Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, actually, it did have an impact, particularly because it was highlighted in the media and it was used to generalise the feeling of fear and a need for Serbs to be particularly alert.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And are you aware of any reports in the western press that have reported ethnic cleansing of Serbs in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I cannot point to any specific information, but I do believe that it was reported and I think it was transmitted, if not straight by journalists, so at least by the High Commission for Refugees, the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, that numbers of people were being displaced in Eastern Slavonia, Serbs among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the United Nations international organisation of countries of Western Europe, that later on helped stop that war, hadn't done anything at that time, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, at that time, the western community was concerned with negotiations, which had been going on for some time. It had been discussed in the European Community. It had been discussed in international agencies based in Europe, but I would say it was paperwork, conferences, discussions. I think everyone thought at that time that this war could be avoided by having peaceful settlement around a conference table.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So it would be reasonable to assume, since ethnic cleansing of Serbs in Slavonia had occurred and some of the official organisations of the European ommunity had reports about that, but it was only expectation that a war should be short-lived. It was reasonable for Serb in Krajina to be apprehensive about it. I am not asking whether they were wrong or right, but was it just reasonable for them to be apprehensive?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I am just trying to focus my answer. I am not trying to make judgments on this, just to assess the situation and my observations. I didn't know if the word "ethnic cleansing" was used already in Eastern Slavonia in early August 1991. I do know that large groups of people, Serbs included, were actually displaced in the course of the fighting between Croats, essentially, and Serbs, essentially. I do know that at a later time, this was used, highlighted, emphasised and I think ordinary people were scared. But still I think that in Prijedor, people were relying on the past. They have had very, very different experience during World War II in terms of having been a Partisan area that was hard hit by non-Partisans. But at that time -- and that has been confirmed by numerous sources. They felt they were standing together and that that togetherness in the past would bring them through whatever difficult times were to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: But that is your conclusion about that they felt they were in a Noah's Ark, so to speak, just because they had a partisan in the midst of World War II and without paying attention of the current events in the rest of their country?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Yes and no. I think, yes, they did pay attention to what was happening elsewhere. Yes, I think most people were very concerned about there being a war. Yes, I think they followed that very intensely. But, no, I don't think they were also afraid of being hunted -- they didn't feel as hunted by the past experiences of one group of people locally against another. They had a different background and experience which made it more easy for them to relate to their neighbours than for Serbs in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would like to introduce Defence Exhibit No. 1. And I know, Your Honours, that this is not being done to question the credibility of this witness, but just to contradict the validity of underlying data on which she is basing her statements. This is the book by Samuel P. Huntington professor at Harvard University, that's dealing on page 283, he is dealing with this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got photocopies for us so we can look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I will make some photocopies, but I was thinking if you can put it on the overhead projector and say the sentences, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will need photocopies of it, but you can put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Excuse me for turning my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could get a little bit clearer picture, just to the usher.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I'm just pointing to it so that, perhaps, they can zoom in on it. I think this will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you've got it.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: Would you like me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could read the first two sentences on the full paragraph that is in the full view here, starting with --

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: "Western support for Croatia also included overlooking the ethnic cleansing and the violation of human rights and the laws of war for which the Serbs were regularly denounced. The West was silent when in 1995, the revamped Croat army launched an attack on the Serbs of Krajina, who had been there for centuries, and drove hundreds of thousands of them into exile in Bosnia and Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is enough. So it's reasonable to assume that your data that you looked at this problem and research that Professor Huntington has done are obviously differing. Because your conclusions and his conclusions are two different conclusions.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I think I shall disagree with him in his first sentence. The second is after.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, what I asked, I'm not questioning your opinion, nor putting his opinion against your opinion. What I'm asking is, is it reasonable for you to conclude that the data upon which he has relied on the same issue that you here testified about, it's different than yours?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: You asked me previously if I was aware of reports in the western press concerning Eastern Slavonia, to which I testified that I could not recall any in particular, but I was aware that, for instance, the High Commission for Refugees had drawn attention to this. And since I have not studied this, in particular, I am unable -- I don't think I can be seen as an expert on what the western press or those who may be included in the sentence "Western support for Croatia," whether or not it was like this or that. I think it's beyond me to be able to make assessments on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I will continue with the next line of questioning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So it would be more reasonable -- it would be reasonable to conclude that Serbs in Prijedor were apprehensive of what the future might bring to them, and their conclusions about brotherhood are, indeed, a little bit more proper looked at in hindsight than yours, because ethnic cleansing happened in Krajina in a large scale, and western experts in western states didn't respond at all.

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: The reference to Krajina and the Serbs of Krajina is dated 1995. That's three years -- it's August 1995, I tend to remember. That is three years after the events in Prijedor. Obviously what the people were feeling, I have made a general assessment, their feelings are the real thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm directing your attention now to the Prosecutor's Exhibit 29. That newspaper account when read in its totality indicates that there was some criticism, public criticism, that was rendered against the police and chief of police at that time, Delic, was answering to the criticism. Isn't that your import of the article?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That is absolutely so, and the criticism was that strongly against, essentially, all the authorities in Prijedor, that the High Commissioner’s Office for Refugees and ICRC were approached by people who wanted to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what he is doing, he's basically blaming the police in Prijedor were in control of many, many items of property that were stored at Keraterm, because within the context of this article, they are not talking about human beings in prison there. They are talking about property stored at that facility?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that property somehow disappeared?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: That is also correct. But it is stated explicitly that there is the cooperation between the police, the army and the authorities that still govern.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is it unreasonable to assume that a country at war, there is going to be some degree of cooperation between military police and civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I would assume that any country that is at war would try to unite forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's a reasonable assumption?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To perform the functions that are actually overlapping to support the war effort?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: To work together to a lesser or larger degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in commenting on Exhibit 30 some statements that at that time Colonel Radmilo Zeljaja remained. Do you know what was his rank at the time when the conflict in Prijedor erupted?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I think he was the major. He was --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: A major?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: A major, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you made some comments earlier when you testified about Jasenovac, you brought up the name of Mr. Kurt Waldheim?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In your readings of the paper that were not available to the public, do you recall what was his rank at that time, Mr. Waldheim's?

utterances.speaker: SOPHIE HANNE GREVE
utterances.text: I don't recall his rank. I remember that he was described as the second in line in command within the intelligence unit in Banja Luka, and he was an Austrian, and he worked within the German/Austrian structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So in that region, it seems that perhaps if he was a major at that time, it seems in that region, even not so high ranks of a major could command a great deal of military authority?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we are straying from the point to be dealing with Colonel Waldheim.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
